Had she discovered that her sister wished to deprive her of such expectations and such actual pleasures, what feelings would have possessed her? Only her mother could have comprehended them, for her own might have been nearly identical. Lydia’s visit to Brighton alone comforted her under the sorrowful certainty that her husband never meant to go himself.

Neither, however, knew anything of what had occurred, and their transports continued almost uninterrupted until the day Lydia departed.

Elizabeth was now to encounter Mr. Wickham for the last time. Frequent meetings since her return had largely quieted her agitation; whatever arose from her old preference had vanished altogether. Even in the gentleness that once charmed her, she now detected an artificial uniformity that wearied and repelled. His current manner towards her furnished another cause of displeasure. The readiness he soon showed to resume the attentions of their earliest acquaintance could, after everything that had happened, do nothing but offend her. Finding herself chosen for this empty, trifling gallantry destroyed her remaining concern for him. While firmly discouraging it, she felt the rebuke implied by his assumption that, however long he had neglected her, and for whatever reason, he could gratify her vanity and regain her preference whenever he chose to renew his attentions.

On the regiment’s final day in Meryton, he and several other officers dined at Longbourn. Elizabeth felt so little inclination to part amicably that, when he asked how she had spent her time at Hunsford, she mentioned that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had stayed three weeks at Rosings, and inquired whether he knew the former.

He appeared astonished, annoyed, and alarmed; but after an instant’s recollection his smile returned. He replied that he had often met him formerly, remarked upon his gentlemanly character, and asked how she had liked him. She answered with warm approval. Soon afterward, with a show of indifference, he added, “How long did you say he remained at Rosings?”

“Almost three weeks.”

“And you met him often?”

“Yes, nearly every day.”

“His manners differ greatly from his cousin’s.”

“Very greatly; but I find Mr. Darcy improves as one knows him.”

“Indeed!” Wickham exclaimed, with an expression she did not miss. “And might I inquire—” He checked himself, then continued more cheerfully, “Is it his manner that improves?

Meanwhile, gravity would steadily weaken in inverse proportion to the square of the distance. My speed would therefore increase enormously until I eventually entered the distant region where the moon’s attraction would overcome the earth’s. Based on this reasoning, I saw no point in weighing myself down with more than forty days’ provisions.

“One further difficulty, however, still caused me some uneasiness. It has been observed that people ascending to considerable heights in balloons suffer more than painful breathing. They experience severe discomfort in the head and body, frequently accompanied by nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms, all becoming more troublesome as the altitude increases. This was a disturbing thought. Was it not likely that these symptoms would worsen without limit, or at least until death ended them? I finally concluded otherwise. Their cause was the gradual removal of normal atmospheric pressure from the body’s surface and the resulting swelling of blood vessels near the skin. They did not result from any actual breakdown of the body’s systems. Breathing difficulties were different: in that case, the air’s density was chemically inadequate to renew the blood properly in a ventricle of the heart. Apart from the failure of this renewal, I could therefore see no reason life could not continue even in a vacuum. The expansion and contraction of the chest, ordinarily called breathing, is purely muscular activity: the cause of respiration rather than its effect. In short, I believed that as my body adjusted to the absence of atmospheric pressure, the pain would gradually diminish. Until then, I confidently trusted my exceptionally hardy constitution to withstand it.

“Thus, with your Excellencies’ permission, I have described some, though far from all, of the considerations that persuaded me to undertake a journey to the moon. I will now present the outcome of an attempt so apparently daring in its conception and, in any case, utterly without precedent in human history.

“On reaching the altitude mentioned earlier, three and three-quarter miles, I tossed a quantity of feathers from the basket. They showed that I was still ascending quickly enough, so releasing any ballast was unnecessary. I was pleased, because I wanted to keep as much weight aboard as I could carry, for reasons I will explain later.

I then visited one shop after another, buying what was needed to alter his appearance. Once that was done, I headed to Little Britain on my own business. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk, but immediately rose when he saw me and stood in front of the fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I replied. I had thought carefully on the way about what I meant to say.

“Don’t incriminate yourself,” Mr. Jaggers said, “and don’t incriminate anyone else. Understand—anyone. Tell me nothing. I don’t want to know anything. I’m not curious.”

Naturally, I realized he knew the man had arrived.

“All I want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “is confirmation that what I’ve been told is true. I have no hope that it is false, but at least I can verify it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “Did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” He tilted his head, looking at the floor rather than at me, as though listening to it. “‘Told’ seems to suggest a spoken conversation. You can’t have a spoken conversation with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“Then I’ll say ‘informed,’ Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“A person named Abel Magwitch has informed me that he is the benefactor whose identity has been hidden from me all this time.”

“That is the man,” Mr. Jaggers said, “in New South Wales.”

“And nobody else?” I asked.

“Nobody else,” said Mr. Jaggers.

“I’m not unreasonable enough to hold you responsible for my mistakes or false conclusions, sir. But I always believed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” Mr. Jaggers replied, turning his cool gaze on me and biting his forefinger, “I bear no responsibility for that.”

“And yet everything seemed to point to her, sir,” I pleaded miserably.

“Not a scrap of evidence, Pip.” He shook his head and gathered his coat around him. “Trust nothing on appearances. Base everything on evidence. There is no better rule.”

After a short silence, I sighed. “I have nothing more to say. I have confirmed my information, and that is all.”

“Now that Magwitch—in New South Wales—has finally revealed himself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you will appreciate, Pip, how strictly I have confined myself to facts in every communication with you. I have never strayed even slightly from the facts. You understand that?”

“Completely, sir.”

“When Magwitch—in New South Wales—first wrote to me—from New South Wales—I warned him that he must never expect me to depart from the strict facts.
